Beating brain cancer

By: Eugene Botha | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
........new medical breakthrough that could cure brain cancer

Unique Selling Point:
Medical technology that affects all our lives -- all of us are at risk for brain tumors

Summary:
In a new landmark study, researchers from the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill were able to convert skin cells into cancer-hunting stem cells that homed in and destroyed glioblastoma brain tumors. The investigators are optimistic that this technique could provide a significantly more effective treatment for the disease, which typically has a poor long-term survival rate.

Further information:
New Cancer Breaktrough: Turning Skin Cells into Cancer Hunters
In a new landmark study, researchers from the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill were able to convert skin cells into cancer-hunting stem cells that homed in and destroyed glioblastoma brain tumors. The investigators are optimistic that this technique could provide a significantly more effective treatment for the disease, which typically has a poor long-term survival rate.

"Patients desperately need a better standard of care," remarked senior study author Shawn Hingtgen, Ph.D., assistant professor in the UNC Eshelman School of Pharmacy and member of the Lineberger Comprehensive Care Center.

The survival rate beyond two years for patients with a glioblastoma is only 30 percent due to its difficulty to treat. Moreover, even if surgical intervention removes the bulk of the tumor, it's next to impossible to get the invasive, cancerous branches that spread deeper into the brain, which inevitably lead to regrowth. Sadly, most patients die within a year and a half of their diagnosis.

The investigators built upon previous Nobel Prize–winning research that allowed them to turn skin cells—specifically fibroblasts—into embryonic-like stem cells. Their goal was to develop a new personalized treatment for glioblastoma that starts with a patient's own skin cells, with the aim of destroying the deep cancerous tendrils, effectively killing the glioblastoma.

The UNC researchers were successful in reprogramming fibroblasts to become induced neural stem cells (iNSCs). Working with mice, the research team showed that the neural stem cells had the ability to move throughout the brain, home in on, and kill any remaining cancer cells. Additionally, the researchers demonstrated that these stem cells could be engineered to produce a tumor-killing protein, adding another blow to the cancer.

“We find that iNSCs genetically engineered with optical reporters and tumoricidal gene products retain the capacity to differentiate and induced apoptosis in co-cultured human glioblastoma cells,” the authors wrote.

“Time-lapse imaging shows that iNSCs are tumoritropic, homing rapidly to co-cultured glioblastoma cells and migrating extensively to distant tumor foci in the murine brain.”

The findings from this study were published recently in Nature Communications through an article entitled “Therapeutically engineered induced neural stem cells are tumour-homing and inhibit progression of glioblastoma.”

Amazingly, depending on the type of tumor, the researchers were able to increase survival times in mice between 160 to 220 percent.

"Our work represents the newest evolution of the stem-cell technology that won the Nobel Prize in 2012," Dr. Hingtgen explained. "We wanted to find out if these induced neural stem cells would home in on cancer cells and whether they could be used to deliver a therapeutic agent. This is the first time this direct reprogramming technology has been used to treat cancer."

Dr. Hingten and his team are looking toward the next steps, which he said will focus on human stem cells and testing more effective anti-cancer drugs that can be loaded into the tumor-seeking neural stem cells.

Press Release:


Brain Cancer Hunters
The glioblastoma is an aggressive form of brain cancer and it’s very difficult to treat. The survival
rate for patients beyond two years, is only 30 percent. But now, a landmark study could reveal the
answers cancer researchers have been looking for. Scientists from the University of North
Carolina have been able to convert skin cells into cancer-hunting stem cells which hone in and
destroy tumours. Carte Blanche witnesses the life-saving possibilities of this medical
breakthrough

Script:


V/O:
These three men are responsible for one of the most amazing medical breakthroughs in cancer treatment in recent years. At the University of North Carolina in Chapel Hill, they have found a way to use simple skin cells to destroy one of the deadliest forms of brain cancer.

Prof Matt Ewend is the Chair of the Department of Neurosurgery and says there are many forms of brain cancer.

Prof. Matt Ewend:
When a patient gets a diagnosis of a brain tumour it can be anywhere from a small benign tumour that can be watched or or easily removed and cured with surgery, all the way to a tumour like the glioblastoma which is a tumour that is generally not curable with surgery, radiation or chemotherapy.

V/O:
Ewend and his group focus on Glioblastoma. It is very common, highly aggressive and kills indiscriminately -- young children, adults and older people. And it can strike anybody at any time.

LINK
It is also particularly deadly and on average, people who get it, die within 14-16 months of the diagnosis.

V/O:
It is also difficult to treat.

Matt:
It is in the brain. So, if you are a surgeon as I am, and you are treating something that is in the lung or colon you can take a foot on the left and a foot on the right and make sure that you have all of the tumour. But in the brain you can’t go a foot on the left and a foot on the right.

V/O:
But despite this, surgeons can remove the glioblastoma tumours successfully. However, this cancer has a further characteristic that makes it virtually incurable – it has a tendency to spread from very early on.

Matt:
Even as a surgeon when I look on an MRI scan and I see the tumour, I see a big white ball on the MRI and I show it to the patient and I say “That’s the tumour”, I know that the tumour has fingers that extend beyond that, that are in the normal brain, and even if I remove everything that look abnormal there will still be tumour cells that are in there.

LINK
So, it is impossible to completely remove all the cancer cells with surgery.

V/O:
And the remaining cells make it possible for tumours to regrow says Prof Shawn Hingtgen.

Prof Shawn Hingtgen:
But what is really interesting is, after surgery the tumour is extremely angry. It comes back. It regrows actually two or three times faster than the tumour before surgery.

V/O:
And strange as it seems, further treatment of this dread disease post-surgery has changed very little over many decades.

Prof Simon Khagi
We still have chemotherapy which hasn’t gone beyond the standard line which is called Temedor or Temezolomide and we have been using that chemotherapy pretty regularly in the treatment of glioblastoma. Radiation has somewhat advanced as well. We have a fairly defined dose for newly diagnosed glioblastoma. So, and that has been the standard of care for the past twenty or so years.

V/O:
Prof Simon Khagi is an oncologist and he says the chemo and radiation merely delays the inevitable. This cancer returns because of the few cancer cells that invariably remain in the brain after surgery.

The team then decided to approach the disease in an alternative way, by working with stem cells. But that was not so simple.

Shawn:
A lot of people have heard of embryonic stem cells which had a lot of controversy because lot of times you had to sacrifice and embryo to do that and it raised a lot of ethical concerns, religious concerns, things around that and there were a lot of constraints on stem cell research for a number of years.

LINK
But things changed drastically when the Nobel Prize for medicine was awarded to two scientists in 2012.

V/O:
They were Sir John Gurdon and Prof Shinya Yamanaka and they had shown it was possible to take mature skin cells and turn them into stem cells. Suddenly embryonic stem cells were not needed anymore.

Shawn:
This skin flipping, reprogramming technology actually allowed you to accomplish many of the same tasks and promises that the embryonic stem cell technology offered but without any of those ethical concerns because you simply start with skin going backwards and basically making something that looks like an embryonic stem cell but it simply comes from your skin.

V/O:
To turn skin cells into a stem cells it is necessary to reset the genome of the cell by adding certain master regulator genes to the DNA of the cell. They use viruses to carry these genes into individual cells.

Shawn:
The advantage of a virus is that it is very good at infecting cells. People are familiar with viruses – they are really good at infecting you, so what we are able to do is to take all the nasty bits that make you sick out of the virus and we put in the genes of interest that we want. So that when we introduce the virus onto the cells instead of infecting and making you sick it will actually insert those genes, the genes for the cell conversion into the genome of your skin.

LINK
With their particular interest in the brain the team stared to produce brain stem cells, or induced neural stem cells.

V/O:
They knew these neural stem cells have a very peculiar characteristic.

Shawn:
Neural stem cells, cells of your brain will chase cancer. They naturally home to tumours. A lot of people think neural stem cells, they think regenerative medicine and rebuilding the brain and the spine. Turns out there is this aspect of natural stems cells, the cells we all have in our brain that allow them to naturally chase cancer. They can follow the chemotactic signal so the tumour is giving off signals that causes the stem cells to crawl and find them and localize with it. But when they localize with it, they don’t do much. They kind of bump up against the tumour.

V/O:
But this was all they needed. They now had a way to sniff out even single, invisible cancer cells in the brain.

And they had expertise in new cell based technology that enabled them to also add further genes to the modified cells that would make them produce enzymes and agents that are toxic to cancer cells.

Shawn:
We can either have the cells pump out ant-cancer things like anti-bodies, things like that that would bind to the cancer and kill it. Or we can have them carry different enzymes, things inside the cell so that we give an inactive drug the stem cell will actually convert it into an active anti-cancer agent and create a halo of the drug around the cell, so therefor when the cell crawls, finds a tumour, we can turn on the therapy and kill the tumour in that area around it.

V/O:
A special cloth-like material coated with millions of the modified neural stem cells carries the cells into the brain.

Shawn:
And so now what we are actually able to do is that at the time of surgery when the tumour comes out we kind of wall paper or line the surgical cavity with these scaffold stem cell composites and that stabilizes the cells but then allows them to crawl off and the go find the tumours.

V/O:
They can even follow it live as it is happening.

Matt:
We can label the tumour cells so that they will show up red and we can label the stems cells so that they show up green and then we can track and see that the cells will kill the tumour cells. We can see as the stem cells hone in on the tumour cells, the tumour cells die.

V/O:
Here a green coloured stem cell loaded with toxins have found a cancer cell coloured red, and it is killing it within days. Their work with mice has shown that they were able to halt and even reverse tumour growth in mice brains.

This is a massive breakthrough but what are the time-frames?

LINK
The team is cautiously optimistic that it will not take long before the first patients receive the treatment. They recon it will happen within a year from now.

Shawn:
I am always optimistic so we are going to try for a year and we are going to do everything to get there, cause again, looking out the window at the hospital, these patients don’t have the time for us to be slow or to fail so we to be fast and we need to be good at what we do, and so we are going to give it our best shot.
